title: Episode 155: Grover Cleveland and the Panic of 1893: The Gold Crisis and the Morgan Syndicate
description:
Just weeks after Grover Cleveland was inaugurated for his historic non-consecutive second term in March 1893, the American economy plunged into the worst depression the nation had ever experienced. The Panic of 1893 saw six hundred banks collapse, fifteen thousand businesses fail, and unemployment soar to twenty percent. European investors panicked, draining the United States Treasury's statutory gold reserve toward total insolvency. Standing immovable against the populist clamor for free silver, Cleveland fought a vicious battle to repeal the Sherman Silver Purchase Act and summoned financier J. Pierpont Morgan to a tense, secret midnight meeting in the White House to save the nation's gold standard. Discover the harrowing financial crisis that broke the Democratic Party.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we enter the stormy second administration of Grover Cleveland. Returning to the presidency in 1893, Cleveland found a country staring into the abyss of total economic collapse. With the federal treasury days away from bankruptcy and millions of citizens thrown out of work, Cleveland staked his reputation and party unity on defending the gold standard. Here is George with the full story of the Great Panic of 1893.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE STORM BREAKS ON WALL STREET
When Grover Cleveland took the presidential oath on the East Portico of the Capitol on March 4, 1893, a freezing northeaster coated the city in sleet and slush. Cleveland looked out over a crowd shivering under umbrellas and warned in his inaugural address that the nation was approaching financial peril. The warning proved prophetic with terrifying speed. In the late 1880s, an unsustainable speculative bubble in railroad overbuilding, coupled with reckless Wall Street credit expansion, had pushed the American financial system to the brink. On May 4, 1893, the Philadelphia and Reading Railroad and the National Cordage Company collapsed, sending shockwaves through the financial exchanges.\n\nWall Street erupted in panic. In a single morning, stock prices plunged into freefall as brokerage houses went bankrupt. By midsummer, more than six hundred commercial banks had failed across the South and West, locking their doors against mobs of weeping depositors demanding their life savings. Over fifteen thousand businesses collapsed, and four million American workers were thrown out of employment. In major industrial cities like Chicago, New York, and Pittsburgh, lines at soup kitchens stretched for miles. Desperate families scavenged for coal along railroad tracks, and tent cities of homeless workers sprang up on the outskirts of towns. It was the deepest economic catastrophe in the history of the Republic.\n\nIn rural communities across the Midwest, foreclosures multiplied by the thousands, leaving once-thriving farming townships bankrupt and driving desperate families toward urban breadlines.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BLEEDING GOLD RESERVE
At the heart of the catastrophe lay a lethal currency defect engineered by Congress: the Sherman Silver Purchase Act of 1890. Under this law, the federal government was legally required to purchase four and a half million ounces of silver every month, paying for it with Treasury notes that could be redeemed in either gold or silver at the option of the holder. Western silver mining interests and southern agrarian populists celebrated the law, believing it inflated the money supply and made it easier for debt-burdened farmers to pay their mortgages. But European investors viewed silver-backed currency with profound dread.\n\nFearing that the United States was preparing to abandon the gold standard and pay its debts in depreciated silver, British, French, and German bankers began dumping American securities on the open market, presenting their Treasury notes to the New York Sub-Treasury and demanding physical gold coin for shipment across the Atlantic. Week after week, ocean liners steamed out of New York Harbor carrying millions of dollars in gold bullion to the vaults of London and Paris. The statutory gold reserve in the United States Treasury, established at a minimum threshold of one hundred million dollars to guarantee the nation's currency, began hemorrhaging rapidly. By April 1893, the reserve dipped below the sacred one-hundred-million-dollar mark.\n\nThe run on gold threatened to destabilize international trade, as foreign shippers demanded payment exclusively in British sovereigns or gold coin before releasing imported merchandise.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BATTLE TO REPEAL THE SILVER ACT
To Grover Cleveland, the issue was black and white: the gold standard was not merely an economic policy, but a sacred moral covenant. To permit the United States to default on its gold obligations or pay its debts in debased silver was, in his eyes, an act of national dishonor and bankruptcy. In June 1893, despite suffering in secret from a life-threatening illness, Cleveland issued a proclamation summoning Congress into an emergency special session on August 7 to repeal the Sherman Silver Purchase Act.\n\nWhat followed was one of the most vicious legislative battles in congressional history. Southern and Western Democrats, led by a young, silver-tongued thirty-three-year-old congressman from Nebraska named William Jennings Bryan, revolted against their own president. Bryan delivered a mesmerizing, three-hour speech on the floor of the House, declaring that the Democratic Party would not bow to Wall Street gold monopolists. But Cleveland was immovable. Wielding federal patronage like a broadsword, the President informed rebellious congressmen that postmasters and federal marshals would be appointed only if they voted for repeal. In the Senate, silver senators launched an exhausting, round-the-clock filibuster that lasted for sixty-one days. Yet Cleveland refused to compromise an inch. On October 30, 1893, the Senate capitulated, passing the repeal by a vote of 43 to 32. Cleveland had won a monumental constitutional victory, but the Democratic Party was permanently shattered into warring ideological halves.\n\nCleveland worked sixteen hours a day throughout the debate, personally telephoning uncommitted senators and insisting that party loyalty took second place to national solvency.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE WINTER OF DESPAIR AND COXEY'S ARMY
Repealing the Silver Purchase Act halted the legal hemorrhage of gold, but it did nothing to cure the underlying depression. As the bitter winter of 1893 descended, millions of unemployed laborers faced starvation. In Massillon, Ohio, an eccentric, wealthy populist businessman named Jacob S. Coxey conceived a dramatic protest: he would lead an army of unemployed workers on a five-hundred-mile march across Ohio and Pennsylvania to the steps of the United States Capitol to demand that Congress pass a five-hundred-million-dollar public works program to build roads and hire the jobless.\n\nChristened 'Coxey's Army'—or the Commonweal of Christ—the marchers set out on Easter Sunday of 1894. Across the nation, newspapers followed their progress with sensational headlines, while copycat armies formed in California, Colorado, and Illinois. When Coxey's ragged force of five hundred men reached Washington on May 1, tens of thousands of spectators lined Pennsylvania Avenue. But when Coxey attempted to climb the marble steps of the Capitol to deliver his petition, mounted police charged the crowd, swinging clubs. Coxey and his lieutenants were arrested—not for insurrection, but for the absurd misdemeanor of walking on the Capitol grass. To millions of working Americans, the Cleveland administration appeared callously indifferent to human misery.\n\nCoxey's peaceful demonstration highlighted the profound gulf between Washington policymakers and the desperate human suffering created by industrial unemployment.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIDNIGHT RENDEZVOUS WITH J.P. MORGAN
By January 1895, the Treasury's gold reserve was melting away at the rate of two million dollars a day. The reserve had plummeted to a terrifying forty-one million dollars; within forty-eight hours, the United States government would be forced to suspend specie payments and default on its debt. In New York, the titan of Wall Street, John Pierpont Morgan, recognized the impending catastrophe. Morgan boarded his private railroad car, steamed to Washington, and walked into the Executive Mansion on the evening of February 7.\n\nCleveland initially refused to see him, fearing that meeting with the symbol of Wall Street capital would destroy him politically. Secretary of the Treasury John G. Carlisle pleaded with the President, and Cleveland finally relented. Around midnight, Morgan sat across from Cleveland in the President's second-floor library, puffing on an enormous Havana cigar. Morgan laid a scrap of telegraph paper on the desk, showing that the Sub-Treasury in New York had only nine million dollars in gold left, and that an investor held a draft for twelve million dollars that would be presented at dawn. 'Mr. President,' Morgan rumbled in his deep voice, 'the United States will default before three o'clock tomorrow afternoon unless you act tonight.' Cleveland asked what could be done. Morgan pulled an obscure, forgotten Civil War statute from his pocket—Section 3700 of the Revised Statutes—which authorized the Secretary of the Treasury to purchase gold with government bonds in an emergency without congressional approval.\n\nMorgan's direct intervention demonstrated the immense financial leverage held by private banking houses over the federal government during the Gilded Age.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SYNDICATE THAT SAVED THE GOLD
Morgan proposed an audacious plan: his banking syndicate, partnered with the House of Rothschild in London, would purchase sixty-five million dollars in United States gold bonds. In return, Morgan pledged that his syndicate would import at least half of the gold from Europe and use their international influence to halt all gold exports from the United States until the currency was stabilized. Cleveland was cornered; Congress was deadlocked and refused to authorize new gold bonds. He looked at Morgan and said: 'If you can guarantee that the gold will stay in the Treasury, I will accept your terms.'\n\nMorgan kept his word. The European Rothschild gold arrived in heavy oak casks unloaded under armed guard at New York wharves. The syndicate sold the bonds at a handsome profit, but they achieved the impossible: the run on the Treasury halted instantly, foreign confidence returned, and the gold reserve rebounded to over one hundred million dollars. Yet when the details of the contract were disclosed, populists and silver Democrats erupted in radioactive fury. They accused Cleveland of selling the sovereignty of the American Republic to Jewish and Wall Street bankers for private profit. Cleveland was burned in effigy across the South and West, reviled by his own party as a traitor who had knelt before J.P. Morgan.\n\nDespite ferocious populist condemnation, the bond contract achieved its objective, preserving the credit of the United States without a single day of default.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BITTER ISOLATION OF AN HONEST MAN
The defense of the gold standard was Grover Cleveland's finest hour of moral courage, and his absolute political ruin. He had prevented international bankruptcy and maintained the credit of the United States, but he had alienated the great mass of his party. When the Democratic National Convention met in Chicago in 1896, silver populists seized total control. William Jennings Bryan electrified the delegates with his immortal 'Cross of Gold' speech, thundering: 'You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns; you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold!'\n\nThe convention formally repudiated the sitting Democratic President, refusing even to pass a customary resolution praising his administration. Cleveland spent the final year of his presidency in complete political isolation, abandoned by his party and unforgiven by the populist movement. Yet he never wavered in his conviction. Retiring to Princeton, New Jersey, in 1897, Cleveland watched as the nation returned to prosperity under William McKinley's administration, vindicating the gold standard he had saved. Grover Cleveland had sacrificed his political life to save the financial honor of the United States, proving to the end that he would rather be right than be popular.\n\nCleveland's unwavering defense of sound currency preserved the economic foundation that enabled the extraordinary industrial expansion of the twentieth century.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Grover Cleveland's defense of the gold standard in the Panic of 1893 was a remarkable demonstration of immovable executive fortitude under unimaginable pressure. He saved the credit of the nation at the cost of his own political future. Next week, we explore the shocking secret of that same summer: Cleveland's covert cancer surgery aboard the yacht Oneida, and his dramatic deployment of federal troops in the Pullman Strike of 1894. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
